content: Ebola virus RNA has been detected at low levels in the breast milk of Ebola survivors for up to 16 months after the onset of symptoms. Additionally, spontaneous galactorrhea has been reported in female survivors, with one case showing detectable Ebola virus RNA in breast discharge nine months post-symptom onset. Further research is required to determine the exact duration and infectivity of Ebola virus persistence in breast milk. Due to the potential risk of viral persistence in breast milk, lactating Ebola survivors are advised to have their breast milk tested for Ebola virus RNA using PCR. Testing should be conducted immediately upon discharge from the Ebola Treatment Unit (ETU). Lactating women who are unaware of their breast milk status or whose milk tests negative for Ebola virus RNA should continue breastfeeding. However, if Ebola virus RNA is detected, breastfeeding should be suspended, and breast milk should be retested every 48 hours until two consecutive negative results are obtained. During this period, breast milk should be replaced with a sustainable and appropriate breast milk substitute, preferably a liquid formula that does not require reconstitution with water, as it poses less risk than powdered infant formula. Proper hygiene of feeding utensils, adequate supplies for the infant's needs, and access to healthcare services are essential. Mothers should be counseled on minimizing the risks associated with formula feeding and supported in maintaining breast milk production to enable resumption of breastfeeding once two consecutive negative milk samples are confirmed. Psychosocial support should also be provided to the mother and family as needed. To facilitate the resumption of breastfeeding, mothers should be taught and supported to express breast milk regularly, either manually or with a breast pump, following Ebola infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines to minimize the risk of virus transmission. Infants who have been breastfed by a mother with PCR-positive milk should be monitored as close contacts for 21 days from the last day of breastfeeding. Lactating Ebola survivors with PCR-positive or untested breast milk should practice strict hand and personal hygiene, including thorough washing with soap and water after any contact with breast milk. Feeding utensils should be disinfected with a 0.5% chlorine solution for approximately 15 minutes. Counseling and support for infant feeding should be tailored to the infant's age. Sexually active female Ebola survivors should receive counseling on family planning, contraception, and prevention of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) at discharge. Women of reproductive age should be assessed for amenorrhea during their first follow-up clinic visit and at subsequent visits. If a female survivor experiences amenorrhea for more than four weeks, including time spent in the Ebola treatment facility, a urine or blood pregnancy test should be conducted. Pregnant survivors should receive antenatal, delivery, and postnatal care in accordance with WHO and national standards. Arrangements should be made for immediate transfer to an ETU with facilities for safe delivery and neonatal care if needed. Deliveries should be conducted in full personal protective equipment (PPE), and products of conception (e.g., amniotic fluid, placenta, neonate) should be tested for Ebola virus RNA using PCR. Ebola survivors may experience persistent or new symptoms during convalescence, which can begin early in recovery or within the first three months. A system for follow-up clinical and psychosocial/mental health care should be established for these patients. Survivors should receive psychological and social support counseling before discharge and during regular follow-up visits. If significant mental health issues are identified, referral to a mental health care provider may be necessary. All patients should have at least one follow-up clinical and psychosocial health assessment within two weeks of discharge and be provided with clear instructions on whom to contact for any problems or questions. A comprehensive history and physical examination, including rheumatologic, ocular (e.g., visual acuity), nutritional, and mental health screenings, should be performed early after discharge. Continued psychological and social support should be provided as needed. Ocular symptoms, such as eye pain, conjunctivitis, photophobia, hyperlacrimation, uveitis, and visual impairment, require urgent attention. Uveitis, if untreated, can progress to severe visual impairment or blindness. Neurological complications, including tinnitus and hearing loss, have been reported in up to 27% of survivors. Skin disorders, such as generalized dry skin, pruritus, and desquamation, particularly on the extremities, palms, and soles, have also been variably reported. During an Ebola or Marburg outbreak, case definitions may be adapted to reflect new clinical presentations or transmission modes specific to the local context. Suspected cases include individuals with sudden onset of high fever and contact with an Ebola case, a sick or dead animal, or those presenting with specific symptoms such as headache, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, lethargy, muscle or joint pain, difficulty swallowing, breathing difficulties, or unexplained bleeding. Probable cases include suspected cases evaluated by a clinician or individuals who died from suspected Ebola with an epidemiological link to a confirmed case but without laboratory confirmation. Confirmed cases require positive laboratory results, such as PCR or viral isolation. For routine surveillance in non-outbreak settings, suspected cases involve fever unresponsive to usual treatments and at least one hemorrhagic sign, such as bloody diarrhea or bleeding gums. Confirmed cases require laboratory confirmation. Community-based surveillance should include alert cases, such as sudden deaths or illnesses with fever unresponsive to treatment. Management of dehydration in Ebola patients involves tailored fluid replacement plans (A, B, or C) based on the severity of dehydration. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is recommended for mild cases, with specific instructions on preparation and administration. Severe dehydration requires immediate intravenous (IV) fluids, with reassessment every 1–2 hours to monitor hydration status. If IV fluids are unavailable, nasogastric rehydration with ORS may be initiated.
